SystemSketch · claude/message-communication-view-8061f3 @ 85d8364a · 2026-09-06

The communication view now goes both ways

It already read a wired board as Topic, Stream, Service and Action. This adds the other direction: draw the relationship between two Block surfaces and the ports and cables that spell it are generated for you. Flip to Dataflow and they are simply there — real ports, real wires, no second graph.

Why this closes rather than duplicates

The tempting design is to persist the drawn arrow as its own record and reconcile it with the dataflow later. That is a second graph, and it is exactly what the Async-region work was careful not to build.

Instead the arrow materializes immediately into canonical ports and cables, and the Components view collapses them back into the one arrow you drew — which is what it already did for hand-wired boards. The generator writes the port names the existing strict V1 parser reads, so a drawn Action comes back as the same A1 the parser would have found had you wired it by hand. The two views are inverses because there is only ever one store.

The round-trip unit test is the contract that keeps them honest, and it earned its place immediately: _ turns out to be one of the parser's separators, so move_base came back as move.base. The canonical spelling is dot-joined, and the generator now emits exactly that.

What each arrow generates

Measured from COMMUNICATION_PROTOCOL_LEGS at build time — 6 cables across the three families.

Stream

arrow tail = publisher · head = subscriber

<name>.stream→publisher → subscriber

1 canonical cable

Service

arrow tail = client · head = server

<name>.request→client → server
<name>.response←server → client

2 canonical cables

Action

arrow tail = client · head = server

<name>.goal→client → server
<name>.feedback←server → client
<name>.result←server → client

3 canonical cables

Action deliberately omits cancel. The projection already treats it as a coordination side-channel rather than the work or the outcome, so emitting a fourth cable on every Action would make the common case noisier to pay for the rare one. A hand-wired <name>.cancel pair still parses. topic is not drawable for a different reason: it is what an un-annotated plain data edge already projects as, so offering it would ask which of two spellings you meant.

Four-sided ports

A generated socket goes on the face pointing at the component it talks to, so a stacked pair wires vertically instead of looping around. That needs ports on the top and bottom edges, which is the new optional BlockPort.edge. Absent — the entire existing corpus — keeps the derived rule of input-left and output-right, so no board already written changes by a pixel.

The label geometry is taken directly from Vyuh Node Flow's port-label convention, via the prior-art study in docs/four-sided-port-labels-prior-art-2026-09-06.html: the text stays horizontal and is drawn inward from the socket — below a top port, above a bottom one — centred on the dot, so the outer face stays a clean cable corridor. The study's 12px gap is honoured, then clamped into the body band, because the header and footer own the strips the raw offset would land in. Rotated, staggered and outdented labels are what the study rejects.

It also generalises a decision this app had already made locally: the Loop's item outlet leaves the header's bottom edge and puts its label above the dot so the first downward cable cannot strike through the words.

Browser journey

  • Components mode offers exactly the three drawable patterns, none armed and nothing wired
  • a Stream arrow drawn between two surfaces generates one canonical Async leg named for its publisher
  • a stacked pair puts each generated socket on the facing horizontal rail
  • a Service arrow generates request forward and response back, naming the client by the arrowhead
  • an Action arrow generates goal, feedback and result — and deliberately no cancel leg
  • flipping to Dataflow shows the six real cables the three drawn arrows created
  • the four-sided port label is horizontal and centred on its socket, drawn inward per the Node Flow convention
  • the strict parser reads the generated dataflow back as exactly the three relationships that were drawn
  • renaming a relationship rewrites its port names and keeps every cable bound
  • the armed family toggles off, returning the canvas to ordinary selection
  • leaving the region closes the lens, so an ordinary board has no communication drawing affordance
  • the real browser journey emitted no local console errors

Round-trip unit contract

  • collapses every leg of one relationship under one group name
  • never emits a name the parser would re-read as a different phase
  • gives Service and Action the legs their own validation requires
  • runs return legs back along the drawn arrow
  • leaves cancel out of a drawn Action
  • does not offer topic, which is the parser fallback
  • is deterministic, so re-drawing reuses the same ports
  • separates the phases of one relationship
  • keeps a disambiguating suffix round-trip safe
  • keeps a stream port name as the readable channel

Keeping review artifacts alive — five proposals

Asked in the same breath, and this session proved the point the hard way: a crash mid-run killed every retained review on the machine at once, including the one this work builds on. These are ordered by how much they actually buy.

  1. 1A user systemd unit, not a shell child

    The single highest-value change. scripts/review_runtime.py already pins a commit and a worktree; today it starts a process that dies with the machine. Registering each retained review as a systemd --user unit with Restart=always, plus loginctl enable-linger, makes reviews survive reboot, logout, and agent crash. Everything else here is second-best to this.

    Why it helps: This session's own crash killed every one of the ~40 retained reviews at once. That is the failure mode, reproduced.

  2. 2One always-on index page instead of N ports

    A single long-lived server on one well-known port (say 4599) that lists every retained review and reverse-proxies to them on demand, starting a backend lazily on first request. One bookmark that is always alive beats forty URLs that each might not be. It also ends port exhaustion — the pool is currently 4600–4698 and was recently full.

    Why it helps: You never have to remember which port a report was on, and a cold review costs one page load rather than an agent round-trip.

  3. 3Make the report a file, not a service

    Reports are already self-contained HTML with assets inlined. Nothing about them needs a server — a file:// link works forever, offline, with zero processes. Reserve the running server strictly for the interactive board, which genuinely needs the app. Splitting the two means the argument always survives even when the demo does not.

    Why it helps: Half of what dies today did not need to be alive in the first place.

  4. 4A liveness contract in the handoff itself

    Every handoff that cites a URL also states the restart command for that exact endpoint, and the agent health-checks the URL as its last action before reporting. If the check fails, the handoff says so rather than shipping a dead link. Cheap, and it converts a silent rot into a visible one.

    Why it helps: You stop discovering deadness by clicking; the report tells you, and tells you the one command that fixes it.

  5. 5A watchdog that restarts what should be up

    A small periodic job reads the retained-review registry, health-checks each entry marked retained, and restarts the ones that should be up. It is the belt to systemd's braces and it also catches the case systemd cannot: a server that is running but serving a broken build.

    Why it helps: Covers crash, OOM, port theft, and bad-build cases in one place, with a log you can read after the fact.

Decision surface

  • Done and proved. Draw Stream / Service / Action between Block surfaces; generated ports and cables; the Dataflow round trip; four-sided port rails with Node Flow labels; rename in place. 12 browser checks, 11 unit tests, full npm run check green, and the shipped Async-region and communication-focus journeys still pass.
  • Needs you. Two product calls I made and would reverse on a word: Action generates three legs rather than four (no cancel), and a new relationship is named after the publisher for a Stream but the server for a Service or Action. Default if you say nothing: both stand.
  • Deliberately not done. No delete-cascade — undo removes a whole drawn relationship in one step, but deleting one collapsed arrow later removes only that leg and leaves its ports. No topic arrow. No source analysis: this is still V1 strict port-name inference, and the descriptor's provenance field remains the V2 seam.
  • Not integrated. Committed to claude/message-communication-view-8061f3 only. Nothing merged, pushed, or promoted.
